name: Snail mucin

lead: Snail mucin, also called snail secretion filtrate, is the mucus of snails (often Cornu aspersum) used in serums, essences and creams, especially in Korean skincare. Its reported components include allantoin, glycolic acid, hyaluronic acid-type glycosaminoglycans, proteins and peptides.

Reviews describe uses in hydration, anti-aging, acne, scarring and hyperpigmentation, but say most studies are preclinical or small and call for larger trials. A 2022 randomized trial examined a serum with snail secretion filtrate in mask-related acne.

paras: The proposed actions come from its mixture of ingredients: humectant and exfoliating compounds that may support hydration and surface smoothness, and proteins and peptides that cell and animal studies link with antimicrobial, antioxidant and wound-healing effects.

Reviews flag skin irritation, sensitisation and allergic reactions as possible, and note that standardised formulations and formal toxicology monographs are lacking. Product labels typically advise external use only and avoiding the eyes. A case report series on adolescents trying viral skincare trends is cited as a caution about social media skincare products generally.

lead: Snail mucin, or snail secretion filtrate (SSF), is a mucus secretion of snails used as a cosmetic ingredient, particularly in Korean skincare [1][2]. It has been described as a mixture containing allantoin, glycolic acid, proteins, glycosaminoglycans, enzymes, peptides and trace minerals [3].

Reviews list cosmetic uses including anti-aging, hydration, anti-acne, scarring and hyperpigmentation treatments, and medical research interest in antimicrobial, wound-healing, and drug-delivery applications. They also state that most studies have been preclinical or small clinical studies and call for larger trials [2][4].
Published studies did not include looksmaxxing forum discussion of snail mucin, so its place in those communities is not documented here.
infobox: Allantoin, glycolic acid, glycosaminoglycans, proteins, polyphenols [3]
No formal toxicological monographs exist, per a 2025 review [4]

paras: A review of Korean cosmeceutical ingredients lists snail mucin among bioactive animal-derived ingredients with potential applications in skin rejuvenation and wound healing, and says further research is needed [1]. A 2024 review reports cosmetic uses for anti-aging, hydrating, anti-acne, scar and hyperpigmentation purposes, and notes that the global market was estimated in the hundreds of millions to over a billion dollars [2].
A product label for a snail-secretion cream with ginseng and collagen lists use as a facial cream applied and massaged until absorbed [5].

Reviews describe investigation of snail mucin as an antimicrobial, antitumour and wound-healing agent, a biomaterial coating and a drug-delivery vehicle [2][6]. A 2025 review focuses on scar therapy and wound healing, citing allantoin, glycolic acid and hyaluronic acid among the compounds thought to be relevant [4].

A 2022 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial evaluated a facial serum containing snail secretion filtrate together with Calendula officinalis and Glycyrrhiza glabra root extract for face-mask-related acne ('maskne') [7]. The combination product makes it difficult to attribute any result to snail mucin alone.

Beyond that, the reviews characterise the human evidence as small clinical studies and say large-scale trials are needed [2][4]. Laboratory and animal work includes a mouse wound-healing model, a mouse gastric ulcer model, and cell studies in canine keratinocytes, which are not studies of human appearance outcomes [8][9][10].

A 2025 review says that safety concerns such as skin irritation, sensitisation and allergic reactions underline the need for toxicological evaluation, and that no formal toxicological monographs exist, though regulatory frameworks emphasise safety substantiation for snail-mucin products [4]. Product labelling for a cream with snail secretion filtrate advises external use only and avoiding eye contact [5].

A 2024 dermatology article on social media and adolescent behaviour describes cases of adolescents presenting to pediatric dermatology after trying skincare products promoted by 'skinfluencers'; it concerns the broader trend rather than snail mucin specifically [11].

A 2025 review of Cornu aspersum mucus describes antibacterial, antioxidant, proliferative, pro-migration and angiogenesis-promoting effects of its components and discusses chemical variability of the mucus as a source for cosmetic and pharmaceutical products [12]. The 2025 scar review notes a lack of standardised formulations [4].
